9679: Sacramental view: loss and restoration of grace (Catholic and Orthodox)
9680:
Catholic teaching holds that justifying grace, first given in baptism, makes the believer truly righteous and an heir of eternal life, but that it can be lost by mortal sin: a grave matter committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent. Mortal sin destroys charity in the heart and, if unrepented, leads to eternal separation from God. Grace lost can be restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance, which the Council of Trent, following earlier tradition, called a second plank after shipwreck. No one can know with certainty, apart from special revelation, that they will persevere to the end; final perseverance is a gift to be prayed for, and hope, not presumption, is the right attitude.

Orthodox theology frames salvation as a lifelong process of union with God (theosis) begun in baptism and chrismation, sustained by the eucharist and repentance (confession), and capable of being abandoned. Orthodox teachers often summarize this by saying a Christian has been saved, is being saved and hopes to be saved. Both traditions see the warnings as addressed to genuine believers and the promises as God's faithfulness to those who remain in communion.

9689:
The early church faced the question practically: what of baptized Christians who denied Christ under persecution or committed grave sins? The Shepherd of Hermas (second century) allowed one repentance after baptism. Cyprian and others developed public penance; Novatian's rigorist schism (251) refused restoration to the lapsed and was rejected. Penitential practice developed from public, once-only penance to private, repeatable confession by the early Middle Ages.

Trent's Decree on Justification (1547) answered Protestant teaching on assurance and perseverance, and the 1992 *Catechism of the Catholic Church* restates mortal and venial sin, penance and hope. Orthodox churches never had a Reformation debate on the subject, but their liturgy, monastic literature and practice of confession presuppose that grace can be forfeited and recovered.

9837: After a person comes to faith, how does God make them holy: through lifelong, gradual growth that is never complete in this life, through a second definite work of grace that brings perfect love, through a crisis of surrender followed by a life of resting faith, through a subsequent baptism in the Spirit that empowers, or through a lifelong participation in the divine life (theosis)?
9838:
All Christians agree that God calls his people to be holy and that the Holy Spirit is the agent of their transformation. They differ on the shape of the process: whether it is gradual or includes decisive crises, how much victory over sin can be expected in this life, what role human effort plays alongside grace, and what 'holiness' ultimately means.

Five classic answers are compared here. The Reformed view (Westminster Confession chapter 13) teaches progressive sanctification: real but imperfect growth through a lifelong struggle against remaining sin, using ordinary means of grace. The Wesleyan view teaches that, after conversion, believers may receive by faith a second work of grace, entire sanctification or Christian perfection, in which the heart is filled with perfect love; Phoebe Palmer's 'altar theology' made this immediate and accessible, shaping the nineteenth-century Holiness movement. The Keswick or 'Higher Life' view, popularized by Hannah Whitall Smith and the Keswick Convention from 1875, teaches that a crisis of full surrender ushers believers into a life of victory by resting faith, in which the Spirit counteracts the sinful nature. The Pentecostal view centers on a baptism in the Holy Spirit subsequent to conversion that empowers for witness and holy living (Assemblies of God and others), combined with either Wesleyan or progressive views of sanctification. The Orthodox view understands holiness as theosis, a lifelong participation in God's uncreated energies through the sacraments, prayer and ascetic struggle.

These traditions have influenced each other heavily, and many believers hold mixtures of them. The debate matters pastorally: it shapes how Christians understand failure, effort, crisis experiences and expectations of victory.
9840:
The Reformed tradition teaches that sanctification is a work of God's grace, rooted in the believer's union with Christ, in which the whole person is progressively renewed and enabled more and more to die to sin and live to righteousness. It begins decisively at conversion (sometimes called definitive sanctification: the believer has died to sin's reign) and continues throughout life, but it is never complete before death because remnants of corruption remain in every part. The result is a lifelong warfare between flesh and Spirit, in which the Spirit-renewed part prevails over time.

Believers cooperate actively, through mortification (putting sin to death) and vivification (coming alive to God), using the ordinary means of grace: the word, sacraments, prayer, fellowship and discipline. There is no second blessing and no shortcut; growth is real, gradual and uneven. Contemporary voices such as Sinclair Ferguson and Kevin DeYoung stress that justification and sanctification are distinct but inseparable gifts of union with Christ, and that effort in holiness is grace-driven, not opposed to grace.
